newsitem.title: CHINA: HK court snuffs out challenge to constitution.
newsitem.headline: HK court snuffs out challenge to constitution.

text.p: A Hong Kong appeals court on Tuesday crushed a challenge to the legal and constitutional arrangements operating since China resumed sovereignty over the territory four weeks ago.
The Hong Kong government welcomed the court's unanimous ruling favouring the post-colonial administration.

The court dismissed a claim that pre-handover laws had ceased to be valid and said the Provisional Legislature installed by Beijing on July 1 was legitimately created by China's parliament, the National People's Congress (NPC).
The three judges said Hong Kong courts had no jurisdiction to rule on the legality of the chamber as it was appointed by the NPC, the highest body in China.
The court also ruled that a criminal trial linked to a corruption case from which the challenge arose would continue.

Defence lawyers in the criminal case argued that the British Common Law system used in Hong Kong had lapsed with the handover and that the new legislature had failed to formally adopt pre-handover laws, creating a legal vacuum.
But the new government headed by former shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa won on all counts in the first challenge to Hong Kong's post-handover legislature and constitution.
"The Provisional Legislative Council has been validly established under Chinese law and was ratified by the NPC," chief judge Patrick Chan told the packed courtroom.

Chan said there was no question of a legal vacuum after July 1 as Sino-British treaties on the handover had guaranteed the legal framework would continue in Hong Kong, which is now a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China.
"It is clear that the laws previously in force are laws of Hong Kong after July 1," Chan said.
Hong Kong's post-colonial constitution, the Basic Law, derives its authority from the NPC in Beijing, which promulgated it in 1990.
"This court has no jurisdiction to question the legality of the Provisional Legislative Council as it has been appointed by the sovereign," said Justice Gerald Nazareth.
Solicitor-General Daniel Fung, heading the government team of lawyers, welcomed the court's ruling.

"They have given us answers which are comprehensive and which clearly settle many of the controversies that have plagued the inception of the Hong Kong SAR, and we welcome this clearing of the air," Fung told reporters after the judgement.
The government said it was "pleased that the matter is now behind us, and the continuity of our legal system is firmly put beyond doubt", he added.
But the three prominent lawyers who fought against the government said Tuesday's ruling was hardly the end of Hong Kong's problems.

"On whether the Provisional Legislature is legal, it will crop up again in other cases," said lawyer Margaret Ng, who was a member of the now defunct Legislative Council that was supplanted by the provisional chamber.
Another challenge is expected soon when lawyers representing child illegal immigrants will argue that a new law allowing their deportation back to China is a violation of the constitution.
Political commentator Andy Ho welcomed the ruling, but warned of more challenges ahead.

"Most Hong Kong people will agree. They don't want to see a radical ruling on the entire legal and constitutional framework," he said. "But the Hong Kong SAR is facing a more serious challenge on the illegal immigrant issue."
